      {"@context":"http://schema.org","@graph":[{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Ministry of Education New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/educationgovtnz"},"datePublished":"2026-07-06T21:45:08.194Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/educationgovtnz_we-are-proud-to-share-awhi-mai-awhi-atu-activity-7480013994435620865-4guM","text":"We are proud to share Awhi Mai Awhi Atu – Counselling in Schools has been named a finalist in the 2026 Te Hāpai Hapori | Spirit of Service Awards.

Awhi Mai Awhi Atu is a school-based counselling programme that began in 2021, designed to offer evidence-based emotional support for tamariki in primary and intermediate schools. 

It’s about helping young people feel safe, heard, and empowered to succeed both in the classroom and beyond.

In 'Someone to talk to Evaluation of Counselling in Schools' (2024), the Education Review Office found 8 in 10 students (80%) reported improved psychological health after receiving counselling, and students with the most psychological distress have the largest improvement. 

With one parent saying: "My child is changing right before my eyes like a flower blossoming. There've not been so many tantrums anymore. She's not taking it on herself when the grown-ups are having a bad day.” 

SUPPORTING BETTER OUTCOMES 
Awhi Mai Awhi Atu – Counselling in Schools is one of three finalists for Te Tohu mō ngā Hua E Pai Ake Ana | Better Outcomes Award which celebrates the achievement of significant outcomes in areas that matter most for the long-term wellbeing for New Zealanders.​

To find out more, check out the Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho website: https://lnkd.in/e-G6j-DC","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/educationgovtnz_we-are-proud-to-share-awhi-mai-awhi-atu-activity-7480013994435620865-4guM"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Ministry of Education New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/educationgovtnz"},"datePublished":"2026-04-30T22:36:12.004Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/educationgovtnz_latisha-te-%C4%81ti-awa-ng%C4%81ti-tukorehe-ng%C4%81ti-activity-7455746858041241600-zhsq","text":"Latisha (Te Āti Awa, Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Toa Rangatira, Kuki Airini) has used learning as a way to reconnect with her reo, strengthen her Māoritanga and bring kaupapa Māori into nursing and leadership.

From Kōhanga Reo to kura kaupapa, te reo Māori shaped how Latisha understood the world. “It was the language I lived and learned through, it’s how I made sense of my responsibilities as Māori,” she says.

That pathway continued into tertiary study, where she completed the Bachelor of Nursing Māori at Whitireia and WelTec, drawn to a programme centred on Māori perspectives of hauora.

In 2023, Latisha returned to Māori‑centred learning at Te Wānanga o Raukawa, completing Poutāhū Whakahaere, a kaupapa Māori management programme. She continues her studies through Tāhuhu Whakahaere and Ngā Manukura clinical leadership, building leadership capability while staying closely connected to clinical practice and whānau.

“I am a Māori nurse, not just a nurse who appears Māori,” she says — a reflection of how education, identity and service are inseparable.

At home, learning continues too, with Latisha and her husband raising their tamariki through Kōhanga Reo and learning alongside them.

🌟 NEiTA Apple Award for Primary: Amelia Meertens, Year 3 and 4 teacher at Matangi School (pictured, left).
🌟 NEiTA Founder’s Principal’s Award for Leadership: Lysandra Stuart, Glenbrook School Principal (right).

Amelia is a team leader, enviro leader and production leader at her rural Waikato primary school, and was recognised for her student-led, inclusive approach to learning. She received a $5,000 professional development grant from the NEiTA Foundation.

“Agency isn’t just about giving students choice,” says Amelia. “It’s about giving them the skills, scaffolds and confidence to make meaningful decisions about their learning. I want them to feel ownership – to know why they’re learning something, and to recognise their successes in ways that matter to them.”

Every afternoon, Amelia’s students gather for reflection time. “We talk about our successes of the day,” she says. “Sometimes it’s academic, and sometimes it’s something like, ‘I didn’t give up when the puzzle got tricky.’ Both matter.”

Lysandra was acknowledged for her work in revitalising principal networks and mentoring emerging leaders across her region, and received a $10,000 grant. She says, “If we want our students to be brave learners, our teachers have to feel brave too. My job is to build that safety, both through clear expectations and through genuine connection.”

The National Excellence in Teaching Awards (NEiTA) celebrate exemplary teaching across Australia and New Zealand.

Jan was presented with the award at the GLN Annual Conference on Friday 13 March.

Jan began her career in education in 1982 when she joined the Department of Education — the start of four decades shaping the Ministry’s legal work. Since 1991, she has led our legal team, first as Manager of Legal Services and now as Chief Legal Advisor.

Throughout her career, Jan has provided steady and principled leadership through some of the most significant shifts in our education system. She has been a trusted source of advice during major legislative reforms, organisational change and the ongoing development of education in Aotearoa. She has also been a trusted anchor during times of crisis, guiding the Ministry through legal challenges arising from natural disasters, public health emergencies and periods of rapid social change.

Colleagues describe Jan as wise, calm and deeply committed to ensuring the education system works for the children and young people it serves. Her expertise, knowledge and humanity have shaped our legal team and supported many people across the organisation.

This award reflects a lifetime of contribution and a legacy that will continue long after Jan’s retirement on 29 May 2026.

Congratulations, Jan, on this well‑deserved award. Applications close 30 April 2026.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/educationgovtnz_apply-today-the-fulbright-distinguished-activity-7437297776184647681-ZNhQ"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Ministry of Education New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/educationgovtnz"},"datePublished":"2026-03-10T03:11:12.699Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/educationgovtnz_at-the-beginning-of-her-career-sandy-pasley-activity-7436971897940144129-T-SW","text":"At the beginning of her career, Sandy Pasley took every opportunity she could to grow. Now, after four decades of teaching, tumuaki and leadership experience, she’s been named a member of the New Zealand Order of Merit for her services to education, and continues to support others to find out what they’re capable of.

“To really learn and grow as a person, it’s important to challenge yourself,” says Sandy. “If you don’t challenge yourself, you’ll never know what you’re capable of doing. You’ve got to take opportunities to develop.”

Sandy is a long-time executive of the Secondary Principals’ Association of New Zealand. In 2015, she was the first female president to be elected, and she became a life member in 2017.

Sandy found belonging to principal associations extremely valuable and enjoyed the chances to get advice on situations she experienced.

“I think the best ways to learn are just talking to each other; it’s important to be open to learning and not think that you need to have all the answers.”

She adds that the role was challenging at times. “You have to make sure that you’re representing all of the sector and thinking about how changes are going to affect everybody.”

Sandy admits she was daunted, but as principal of Baradene College, reminded herself she would tell the students to “step up and not be afraid”. “I thought ‘come on, how could you tell them that and not do it yourself?’.”

After leaving her tumuaki position, Sandy joined the Ministry of Education as leadership advisor, which she describes as a service by principals, for principals. She enjoys being a listening ear and giving principals the courage and encouragement to make decisions.

One of these inspiring educators is Jessica Vader, a primary school teacher whose research shines a light on the power of peer coaching, where teachers support each other through deep, reflective conversations to grow their practice.

Supported by a TeachNZ Study Award, Jessica explored how peer coaching can be embedded and sustained in primary schools. Her research found that when teachers and kaiako have space for this coaching, they feel more supported, connected and empowered to find solutions that work for them and their learners.

Some of Jessica’s key takeaways from her research include:
💭 Coaching works best when it’s regular and structured.
💭 Leadership modelling makes a huge difference.
💭 Tools like the GROW model help keep conversations focused.
💭 Trust, manaakitanga and ako are at the heart of success.

“There’s a lot of power in asking deep questions and inviting others to explore their own solutions,” says Jessica.

To all the women in education across Aotearoa — thank you. Your mahi, your care, and your leadership make a huge difference for our tamariki every single day.

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We are proud to share Awhi Mai Awhi Atu – Counselling in Schools has been named a finalist in the 2026 Te Hāpai Hapori | Spirit of Service Awards.

Awhi Mai Awhi Atu is a school-based counselling programme that began in 2021, designed to offer evidence-based emotional support for tamariki in primary and intermediate schools. 

It’s about helping young people feel safe, heard, and empowered to succeed both in the classroom and beyond.

In 'Someone to talk to Evaluation of Counselling in Schools' (2024), the <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/education-review-office?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Education Review Office</a> found 8 in 10 students (80%) reported improved psychological health after receiving counselling, and students with the most psychological distress have the largest improvement. 

With one parent saying: "My child is changing right before my eyes like a flower blossoming. There've not been so many tantrums anymore. She's not taking it on herself when the grown-ups are having a bad day.” 

SUPPORTING BETTER OUTCOMES 
Awhi Mai Awhi Atu – Counselling in Schools is one of three finalists for Te Tohu mō ngā Hua E Pai Ake Ana | Better Outcomes Award which celebrates the achievement of significant outcomes in areas that matter most for the long-term wellbeing for New Zealanders.

To find out more, check out the <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/te-kawa-mataaho?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho</a> website: <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/e-G6j-DC?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/e-G6j-DC</a></p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Latisha (Te Āti Awa, Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Toa Rangatira, Kuki Airini) has used learning as a way to reconnect with her reo, strengthen her Māoritanga and bring kaupapa Māori into nursing and leadership.

From Kōhanga Reo to kura kaupapa, te reo Māori shaped how Latisha understood the world. “It was the language I lived and learned through, it’s how I made sense of my responsibilities as Māori,” she says.

That pathway continued into tertiary study, where she completed the Bachelor of Nursing Māori at <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/school/whitireia-and-weltec/?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Whitireia and WelTec</a>, drawn to a programme centred on Māori perspectives of hauora.

In 2023, Latisha returned to Māori‑centred learning at <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/school/te-w%C4%81nanga-o-raukawa/?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Te Wānanga o Raukawa</a>, completing Poutāhū Whakahaere, a kaupapa Māori management programme. She continues her studies through Tāhuhu Whakahaere and Ngā Manukura clinical leadership, building leadership capability while staying closely connected to clinical practice and whānau.

“I am a Māori nurse, not just a nurse who appears Māori,” she says — a reflection of how education, identity and service are inseparable.

At home, learning continues too, with Latisha and her husband raising their tamariki through Kōhanga Reo and learning alongside them.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Two New Zealand kaiako were recognised internationally at the trans-Tasman 2025 National Excellence in Teaching Awards (<a class="link" href="https://au.linkedin.com/company/neitafoundation?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>NEiTA</a>) late last year, for their contribution to the profession.

🌟 NEiTA Apple Award for Primary: Amelia Meertens, Year 3 and 4 teacher at Matangi School (pictured, left).
🌟 NEiTA Founder’s Principal’s Award for Leadership: Lysandra Stuart, Glenbrook School Principal (right).

Amelia is a team leader, enviro leader and production leader at her rural Waikato primary school, and was recognised for her student-led, inclusive approach to learning. She received a $5,000 professional development grant from the NEiTA Foundation.

“Agency isn’t just about giving students choice,” says Amelia. “It’s about giving them the skills, scaffolds and confidence to make meaningful decisions about their learning. I want them to feel ownership – to know why they’re learning something, and to recognise their successes in ways that matter to them.”

Every afternoon, Amelia’s students gather for reflection time. “We talk about our successes of the day,” she says. “Sometimes it’s academic, and sometimes it’s something like, ‘I didn’t give up when the puzzle got tricky.’ Both matter.”

Lysandra was acknowledged for her work in revitalising principal networks and mentoring emerging leaders across her region, and received a $10,000 grant. She says, “If we want our students to be brave learners, our teachers have to feel brave too. My job is to build that safety, both through clear expectations and through genuine connection.”

The National Excellence in Teaching Awards (NEiTA) celebrate exemplary teaching across Australia and New Zealand.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We’re proud to share that our Chief Legal Advisor, Jan Breakwell, has received the Solicitor General <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/government-legal-network?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Government Legal Network</a> (GLN) Supreme Award recognising her remarkable 45 years of service to public law, the education sector and the Crown. Jan was presented with the award at the GLN Annual Conference on Friday 13 March.

Jan began her career in education in 1982 when she joined the Department of Education — the start of four decades shaping the Ministry’s legal work. Since 1991, she has led our legal team, first as Manager of Legal Services and now as Chief Legal Advisor.

Throughout her career, Jan has provided steady and principled leadership through some of the most significant shifts in our education system. She has been a trusted source of advice during major legislative reforms, organisational change and the ongoing development of education in Aotearoa. She has also been a trusted anchor during times of crisis, guiding the Ministry through legal challenges arising from natural disasters, public health emergencies and periods of rapid social change.

Colleagues describe Jan as wise, calm and deeply committed to ensuring the education system works for the children and young people it serves. Her expertise, knowledge and humanity have shaped our legal team and supported many people across the organisation.

This award reflects a lifetime of contribution and a legacy that will continue long after Jan’s retirement on 29 May 2026.

Congratulations, Jan, on this well‑deserved award. Ngā mihi nui for everything you’ve contributed to the Ministry and the education sector 🌟 </p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">At the beginning of her career, Sandy Pasley took every opportunity she could to grow. Now, after four decades of teaching, tumuaki and leadership experience, she’s been named a member of the New Zealand Order of Merit for her services to education, and continues to support others to find out what they’re capable of.

“To really learn and grow as a person, it’s important to challenge yourself,” says Sandy. “If you don’t challenge yourself, you’ll never know what you’re capable of doing. You’ve got to take opportunities to develop.”

Sandy is a long-time executive of the Secondary Principals’ Association of New Zealand. In 2015, she was the first female president to be elected, and she became a life member in 2017.

Sandy found belonging to principal associations extremely valuable and enjoyed the chances to get advice on situations she experienced.

“I think the best ways to learn are just talking to each other; it’s important to be open to learning and not think that you need to have all the answers.”

She adds that the role was challenging at times. “You have to make sure that you’re representing all of the sector and thinking about how changes are going to affect everybody.”

Sandy admits she was daunted, but as principal of Baradene College, reminded herself she would tell the students to “step up and not be afraid”. “I thought ‘come on, how could you tell them that and not do it yourself?’.”

After leaving her tumuaki position, Sandy joined the Ministry of Education as leadership advisor, which she describes as a service by principals, for principals. She enjoys being a listening ear and giving principals the courage and encouragement to make decisions.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Today on International Women's Day, we’re celebrating the amazing wāhine who make a difference in education each and every day 🌟

One of these inspiring educators is Jessica Vader, a primary school teacher whose research shines a light on the power of peer coaching, where teachers support each other through deep, reflective conversations to grow their practice.

Supported by a TeachNZ Study Award, Jessica explored how peer coaching can be embedded and sustained in primary schools. Her research found that when teachers and kaiako have space for this coaching, they feel more supported, connected and empowered to find solutions that work for them and their learners.

Some of Jessica’s key takeaways from her research include:
💭 Coaching works best when it’s regular and structured.
💭 Leadership modelling makes a huge difference.
💭 Tools like the GROW model help keep conversations focused.
💭 Trust, manaakitanga and ako are at the heart of success.

“There’s a lot of power in asking deep questions and inviting others to explore their own solutions,” says Jessica.

To all the women in education across Aotearoa — thank you. Your mahi, your care, and your leadership make a huge difference for our tamariki every single day.
